title: What I Actually Use: My 2026 Technical Stack Inventory

cover.alt: Concept illustration of a carefully organized developer toolkit with modules for code, design, content, and deployment.

figures.title: The working stack, from content to deployment
figures.summary: These are the responsibilities assigned to the tools in this inventory.

items.label: Language and runtime
items.detail: TypeScript and JavaScript run through the Node.js ecosystem.

items.label: Content and interface
items.detail: MDX feeds the Gatsby content site; React supplies reusable UI.

items.label: Design control
items.detail: CSS variables hold theme tokens, with Tailwind and Theme UI supporting styling.

items.label: Delivery
items.detail: Git and GitHub track changes; Netlify hosts builds and supporting services.

figures.caption: A responsibility map of the author's stated stack, not a recommendation for every project.

figures.title: When the default stack changes
figures.summary: The project need determines the exception.

items.label: Tiny landing page
items.detail: Plain HTML or Vite avoids a full content-site setup.

items.label: App-like interaction
items.detail: Next.js or Vite with React supports more dynamic behavior.

items.label: Background work
items.detail: The inventory considers Docker on a VPS or AWS Lambda instead of short hosting functions.

items.label: Small data prototype
items.detail: A JSON file or Supabase may be enough for the first version.

items.label: Native mobile experiment
items.detail: React Native is the author's current experiment path.

figures.caption: Exceptions taken from the article's own inventory; tool choices are contextual.
